osmanisches-reich#keyFacts.4: In 1571 the Ottomans lose the naval battle of Lepanto; in 1683 the second siege of Vienna fails, followed in 1699 by the Treaty of Karlowitz.
osmanisches-reich#keyFacts.5: In 1826 Mahmud II dissolves the Janissaries; in 1839 the Edict of Gülhane opens the Tanzimat, followed in 1876 by the first constitution.
osmanisches-reich#keyFacts.6: In 1908 the Young Turks force the restoration of the constitution; on 1 November 1922 the National Assembly in Ankara abolishes the sultanate.
osmanisches-reich#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
At the head of the empire stood the sultan from the House of Osman, whose rule was considered willed by God. There was no fixed rule of succession: all sons were regarded as eligible to inherit, and Mehmed II expressly permitted the victorious claimant to have his brothers killed in order to prevent civil wars. From the early 17th century the throne usually passed to the eldest male relative, and the princes lived secluded in the palace. Since Selim I the sultans also claimed the role of protectors of the holy places and later the title of caliph.

The empire was governed from the Topkapı Palace in Istanbul. The grand vizier presided over the Divan, the imperial council, in which viziers, chief judges and finance officials deliberated on war, taxes and legal cases. Many high dignitaries had entered the sultan's service as Christian children through the levy of boys and were regarded as his servants; their rise depended on merit and favour. Governors administered the provinces, and cavalrymen received land revenues, so-called timars, in return for military service.

From the late 16th century power shifted from the sultan to court factions, sultans' mothers, the Janissaries and grand viziers such as the Köprülü family, which stabilized the empire once more after 1656. After the defeats against the Habsburgs and Russia, the reforming sultans Selim III and Mahmud II began to rebuild the army and administration on European models. The Tanzimat from 1839 created ministries, new law codes and the legal equality of subjects, and the constitution of 1876 a parliament. After 1908 the Young Turk Committee of Union and Progress determined policy and led the empire into the First World War in 1914.
osmanisches-reich#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
Ottoman society was divided into the ruling class of the askeri, meaning soldiers, officials and scholars, and the tax-paying subjects, the reaya. The great majority lived as peasants in villages in Anatolia, the Balkans and the Arab provinces, alongside nomads and a rich urban culture in Istanbul, Cairo, Aleppo, Damascus, Salonica and Sarajevo. In the cities guilds organized crafts and prices, and pious endowments maintained mosques, schools, fountains, soup kitchens and hospitals.

Christians and Jews were tolerated as protected subjects; they paid a poll tax and regulated marriage, inheritance, education and welfare themselves in their religious communities, the millets. After the expulsion from Spain in 1492, numerous Sephardic Jews found refuge in Salonica and Istanbul. At the same time non-Muslims were legally disadvantaged, and the Christian families of the Balkans had to hand over sons for the levy of boys. Slavery was widespread: prisoners of war and captives from the Caucasus, eastern Europe and Africa served in households, palaces and the army.

Under Islamic law women could own property, inherit, sue in court and establish endowments, which many women of the upper class made use of. In the palace harem, the private world of the sultan's family, women such as Hürrem and Kösem gained great political influence; the sultan's mother, the valide sultan, was one of the most powerful people at court. In the 19th century girls' schools, women's magazines and a debate about women's education and rights emerged, in which writers such as Fatma Aliye took part. Coffeehouses, bathhouses and mosque courtyards were places of sociability where news, rumours and stories were exchanged.
osmanisches-reich#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
The Ottoman Empire understood itself as a Sunni Islamic state in which the religious law of the sharia applied alongside the laws of the sultan, the kanun. At the head of the scholars stood the şeyhülislam, who confirmed in legal opinions, the fatwas, that state measures were compatible with Islam. Madrasas trained judges, teachers and preachers, while Sufi orders such as the Mevlevi with their dervishes and the Bektashi, who were closely linked to the Janissaries, shaped popular piety.

Architecture reached its peak in the 16th century with the architect Sinan, who created domed mosques in Istanbul and Edirne that developed the model of the Hagia Sophia further. Calligraphy, book painting, tiles from Iznik, carpets and textiles are among the most important art forms. Court poetry was written in an Ottoman language full of Arabic and Persian words, while folk poets, shadow-puppet players with the figure of Karagöz and storytellers entertained ordinary audiences. Travel writers such as Evliya Çelebi and historians recorded life in the empire.

With printing in Ottoman Turkish, which İbrahim Müteferrika introduced in 1727, and the reform schools of the 19th century, exchange with European knowledge grew. Military and medical schools were founded, the first official newspaper appeared in 1831, and a press developed in which poets such as Namık Kemal spread concepts such as fatherland and freedom. At the same time national ideas spread among Greeks, Serbs, Bulgarians, Armenians and Arabs that called the common roof of the empire into question.
osmanisches-reich#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
In the 16th century the empire controlled the connections between the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. Silk, spices, coffee and cotton passed through Bursa, Aleppo and Cairo, and Istanbul, with several hundred thousand inhabitants, was one of the largest cities in the world. The state was concerned above all with supplying the capital and the army with grain, meat and raw materials, and it fixed prices and export bans.

Agriculture formed the basis of state revenue, which was collected first through the timar system and later through tax farming. European merchants from Venice, France, England and the Netherlands received favourable customs duties and their own jurisdiction through trade privileges, the capitulations. What had originally been a sign of the sultan's generosity became in the 19th century a gateway for European goods, against which local crafts could hardly compete.

Militarily the Ottomans led the way in the use of cannon and firearms in the 15th and 16th centuries, but later fell behind the European powers. In the 19th century the state financed reforms, railways and telegraph lines with loans from Europe, until in 1875 it had to suspend payments and in 1881 a debt administration run by creditors took over important taxes. Railway lines such as the Anatolian Railway and the Hejaz Railway, steamships and ports changed trade and travel, but also created new dependencies on foreign capital.
renaissance-entdeckungen#summary: Between 1400 and 1600, printing, humanism, the voyages to America and India, and the division of the church change Europe's view of the world and connect the continents permanently for the first time.
renaissance-entdeckungen#overview.0: In the 15th century scholars and artists in the Italian city-states such as Florence, Venice, and Rome turned once again to antiquity. This rebirth, the Renaissance, placed the human being and his abilities at the centre. Rich banking families such as the Medici supported painters, sculptors, and architects, and humanism spread a new form of education based on Greek and Latin sources. Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael created works that are still regarded today as high points of European art.
renaissance-entdeckungen#overview.1: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz developed printing with movable metal type. Books thereby became cheaper and quicker to produce, and knowledge spread at a pace previously unknown. Pamphlets, Bibles in the vernacular, and scientific works now reached a broad public. Without printing neither the Reformation nor the new natural science would have advanced so rapidly.
renaissance-entdeckungen#overview.2: At the same time Portuguese and Spanish seafarers sought new routes to the spices and the gold of Asia. Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, Vasco da Gama India in 1498, and between 1519 and 1522 Magellan's fleet circumnavigated the earth for the first time. Spanish conquerors under Cortés and Pizarro destroyed the empires of the Aztecs and the Inca. For the population of the Americas the arrival of the Europeans meant disease, violence, and forced labour; millions of people died, and from the 16th century Africans were carried across the Atlantic as slaves.
renaissance-entdeckungen#overview.3: In 1517 the monk Martin Luther published his 95 Theses against the trade in indulgences. What began as a call for reform of the church led to the division of Western Christendom into Catholics and Protestants. Princes, cities, and peasants used the new teaching for their own ends, and Europe was plunged into wars of religion. The Catholic Church responded to the challenge with the Council of Trent and the Jesuit order.
renaissance-entdeckungen#overview.4: The picture of the cosmos was also set in motion. In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus placed the sun instead of the earth at the centre of the universe, and observation and mathematics gradually took the place of the old authorities. At the end of the 16th century Europe was wealthier, better educated, and at the same time more deeply divided than ever before, and its ships connected all the inhabited continents for the first time.
renaissance-entdeckungen#consequences.0: Printing made knowledge available on a mass scale and created the basis for a public sphere, science, and modern education.
renaissance-entdeckungen#consequences.1: The voyages of discovery joined Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas into a worldwide trading network; plants, animals, diseases, and people were exchanged between the continents.
renaissance-entdeckungen#consequences.2: The conquest of the Americas destroyed the indigenous empires and established centuries of colonial rule as well as the transatlantic slave trade.
renaissance-entdeckungen#consequences.3: The Reformation divided Christendom permanently, strengthened the territorial princes, and set off wars of religion that lasted until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
renaissance-entdeckungen#consequences.4: The Renaissance and the heliocentric view of the world placed the human being, reason, and observation at the centre and prepared the way for the scientific revolution and the Enlightenment.
renaissance-entdeckungen#keyFacts.0: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invents printing with movable type in Mainz; by 1500 some 30,000 titles have been printed in Europe.
renaissance-entdeckungen#keyFacts.1: In 1492 Columbus reaches the Caribbean; in 1494 Spain and Portugal divide the non-European world between them in the Treaty of Tordesillas.
renaissance-entdeckungen#keyFacts.2: In 1517 Luther sets off the Reformation with the 95 Theses, in 1521 he refuses to recant at Worms, and in 1555 the Peace of Augsburg recognizes two confessions in the empire.
renaissance-entdeckungen#keyFacts.3: In 1543 the heliocentric world view of Copernicus and the anatomy of Vesalius appear in the same year, two cornerstones of modern natural science.
renaissance-entdeckungen#keyFacts.4: The Ottoman Empire under Suleiman, the Mughal Empire under Akbar, and the Songhai Empire in West Africa are among the most powerful states of the age.
renaissance-entdeckungen#keyFacts.5: In 1588 the Spanish Armada fails off England; in 1582 Pope Gregory XIII introduces the calendar still in use today.
renaissance-entdeckungen#keyFacts.6: Between 1500 and 1600 European traders already carry off hundreds of thousands of Africans to the Americas as slaves.
renaissance-entdeckungen#sections.0.para: The Italian city-states were the political laboratory of the Renaissance. In Florence the Medici banking family governed from 1434 onwards without crown or title, by skilfully steering offices, elections, and patronage. Venice remained an aristocratic republic with an elected doge, Milan was ruled by dukes, and the pope was at the same time the sovereign of the Papal States. In 1513, in The Prince, Niccolò Machiavelli described soberly how power is won and maintained, and thereby founded modern political thought.

North of the Alps large monarchies grew together. Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon united Spain and completed the Reconquista in 1492 with the conquest of Granada. From 1519 their grandson Charles V united Spain, the Netherlands, Naples, Austria, and the imperial crown and ruled an empire on which the sun never set. France and England consolidated their royal power; in 1534 Henry VIII detached the English church from Rome and made himself its head.

The Reformation became a question of power. Territorial princes such as Electoral Saxony and Hesse used the new teaching to take over church property and authority over the church, and joined together in the Schmalkaldic League in 1531. After war and negotiation, the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 laid down that each territorial ruler determined the confession of his territory. In France, by contrast, the conflict led to eight wars of religion, whose climax was the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572.
renaissance-entdeckungen#sections.1.para: Around 1500 Europe was a society of peasants. About nine out of ten people lived in the countryside, paid dues to landlords and to the church, and in many places were serfs. The population grew again after the plague years, grain prices rose, and the Twelve Articles of the peasants of 1525 show how strongly the rural population felt threatened by new burdens. At the same time the potato, maize, the tomato, and the turkey from the Americas brought new foodstuffs to Europe in the long run.

In the cities, guilds, councils, and patrician families determined life. Craftsmen, merchants, and scholars formed a self-confident bourgeoisie that bought books, endowed schools, and had portraits of themselves painted. Women helped to run households and workshops, but were excluded from the universities and from most guilds; exceptions such as the painter Sofonisba Anguissola or the Reformation writer Argula von Grumbach remained rare. The witch trials, which increased towards the end of the 16th century, affected predominantly women.

For the peoples of the Americas and Africa the age of discoveries meant catastrophe. Smallpox, measles, and influenza, against which the indigenous population had no defences, killed the greater part of the inhabitants of Central and South America within a century. The Spanish system of the encomienda forced survivors to work in mines and on plantations. The Dominican Bartolomé de Las Casas denounced the atrocities and obtained protective laws in 1542, which however were scarcely enforced.
renaissance-entdeckungen#sections.2.para: Humanism was the educational movement of the age. Scholars such as Erasmus of Rotterdam sought in Greek and Latin manuscripts the unadulterated text of antiquity and of the Bible, mocked scholastic hair-splitting, and called for an educated, peaceable Christendom. Greek and Hebrew were taught at the universities, and Erasmus's Greek New Testament of 1516 became the basis for Luther's translation. Printing transformed this scholarly culture into a public debate with pamphlets, satirical prints, and songs.

In art, painters and sculptors sought the laws of nature. Brunelleschi discovered central perspective, Leonardo studied muscles and tendons on corpses, and between 1508 and 1512 Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. North of the Alps, Albrecht Dürer, Hans Holbein, and Pieter Bruegel created works that captured landscape, everyday life, and the portrait in new ways. Towards the end of the century the theatre flourished in London, and William Shakespeare wrote plays that are still performed worldwide today.

Natural research began to replace authorities with observation. In 1543 Andreas Vesalius corrected the anatomy handed down since Galen through dissections of his own, in the same year Copernicus set the earth in motion, and Tycho Brahe measured the heavens with hitherto unequalled precision. The calendar reform of 1582 showed how astronomy and the church could work together. At the same time the church defended its doctrine with the Index, the Inquisition, and the new Jesuit order, which founded schools throughout Europe and in the mission territories.
renaissance-entdeckungen#sections.3.para: Trading houses and banks shaped the economy. The Medici in Florence and the Fuggers in Augsburg financed popes and emperors; in 1519 Jakob Fugger paid for the election of Charles V and controlled copper and silver mining in Tyrol and Hungary. Bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, and networks of branches made financial transactions over great distances possible. Antwerp replaced Bruges and Venice as the most important trading centre of north-western Europe.

The voyages of discovery rested on new technology. The caravel with its triangular sails could tack against the wind, the compass, the astrolabe, and the cross-staff allowed position to be determined on the open sea, and Portuguese schools of navigation collected charts and experience. Heavy ship's guns gave European fleets superiority in the Indian Ocean. Spices, silk, and porcelain from Asia, as well as sugar from the new plantations of the Atlantic islands and Brazil, became the goods of world trade.

Silver flowed from the Americas to Europe. After the discovery of the mines of Potosí in 1545 and Zacatecas in 1546, hundreds of tonnes of silver arrived each year in Seville and went on to Genoa, Antwerp, and by way of Manila as far as China. Prices in Europe rose sharply in the 16th century, which historians call the price revolution. The silver was extracted by indigenous forced labourers and African slaves, whose suffering was the other side of European wealth.
lateinamerika#title: Latin America: colonial era and independence
lateinamerika#summary: After 1492 Spain and Portugal built colonial empires in the Americas that rested on silver, sugar and the labour of Indigenous people and enslaved Africans; in the 19th century the colonies won their independence and, up to the Mexican Revolution, struggled over borders, constitutions and social justice.
lateinamerika#overview.0: With the arrival of Columbus in 1492 a period of violent upheaval began for the inhabitants of the Americas. In the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 Spain and Portugal divided the new lands between themselves without asking the people who lived there. Spanish conquistadors conquered the Aztec Empire in 1521 and the Inca Empire from 1532; introduced epidemics such as smallpox, war and forced labour caused the Indigenous population to shrink by a large share in the 16th century. From 1500 Portugal took possession of Brazil and built up a sugar economy there.
lateinamerika#overview.1: The Spanish Crown organised its world empire into viceroyalties, first New Spain with its capital Mexico and Peru with Lima. Indigenous communities had to pay tribute and perform labour service, for example in the silver mines of Potosí, whose silver reached Seville on fleets and China on the Manila galleon. Critics such as Bartolomé de Las Casas denounced the violence and obtained the New Laws of 1542, which banned the enslavement of Indigenous people but were often circumvented in practice.
lateinamerika#overview.2: For the plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean, European traders carried millions of Africans across the Atlantic. Enslaved people resisted through flight, sabotage and revolts; in Brazil fugitives founded communities such as Palmares, which survived for almost a century. Colonial society developed a hierarchy based on origin and skin colour, headed by Spaniards and Portuguese born in Europe, followed by the American-born Creoles, mestizos, Indigenous people and the enslaved.
lateinamerika#overview.3: In the 18th century reforms by the Spanish Bourbons increased tax pressure and control; in 1780 Túpac Amaru II led the largest Indigenous uprising of the colonial era in Peru. The revolution of the enslaved in Saint-Domingue led to the independence of Haiti in 1804. When Napoleon occupied Spain in 1808, Creoles in the Americas formed governing juntas of their own; in long wars Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín and others won independence for almost all of Spain's mainland colonies by 1825, while Brazil separated from Portugal more peacefully as an empire in 1822.
lateinamerika#overview.4: The young states remained marked by border conflicts, civil wars and the power of military strongmen. After its war with the United States, Mexico lost large territories in the north in 1848, and in the Paraguayan War and the War of the Pacific neighbours fought over land and raw materials. Liberals such as Benito Juárez separated church and state, Brazil abolished slavery in 1888 as the last country in the Americas, and Cuba fought its way free of Spain by 1898. Growing export economies and mass immigration brought prosperity for elites but also new dependencies, against which the Mexican Revolution rose up in 1910.
lateinamerika#consequences.0: Spanish and Portuguese became the main languages of an entire continent, and Catholicism still shapes Latin America today.
lateinamerika#consequences.1: The encounter of Indigenous, European and African cultures created new societies with their own music, cuisine, religious life and art; at the same time racism and the disadvantaging of Indigenous and Black people continue to have effects in the present.
lateinamerika#consequences.2: Silver from Potosí and Mexico, together with sugar, gold and later coffee, linked the Americas with Europe, Africa and Asia and contributed substantially to the emergence of a worldwide economy.
lateinamerika#consequences.3: The independence movements created almost twenty independent states, whose borders largely followed the colonial administrative units.
lateinamerika#consequences.4: Dependence on exporting raw materials, the unequal distribution of land and the growing influence of the United States remained central problems of the region in the 20th century.
lateinamerika#keyFacts.0: In 1494 Spain and Portugal divide the non-European world between themselves in the Treaty of Tordesillas; in 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral reaches Brazil.
lateinamerika#keyFacts.1: In 1521 the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan falls; in 1532 Pizarro captures the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca.
lateinamerika#keyFacts.2: In 1545 the Spaniards discover the silver mountain of Potosí, the richest source of silver in the early modern period.
lateinamerika#keyFacts.3: In 1691 Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz defends the right of women to education in Mexico.
lateinamerika#keyFacts.4: In 1780 the uprising of Túpac Amaru II begins in Peru; in 1804 Haiti becomes independent as the first state founded by formerly enslaved people.
lateinamerika#keyFacts.5: Between 1810 and 1825 the Spanish mainland colonies win their independence; in 1822 Brazil becomes an empire of its own.
lateinamerika#keyFacts.6: In 1888 Brazil abolishes slavery as the last country in the Americas; in 1910 the Mexican Revolution begins.
lateinamerika#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
lateinamerika#sections.0.paragraphs.0: The Spanish Crown regarded the conquered territories as kingdoms of its own, governed from Spain by the Council of the Indies. On the spot, viceroys represented the monarch: the Viceroyalty of New Spain was created in 1535 and the Viceroyalty of Peru in 1542, with New Granada and Río de la Plata added in the 18th century. Courts known as audiencias supervised the administration, and at the end of each term of office an official was held to account in a formal review. Because letters to Spain took months, colonial authorities had considerable leeway in practice, and laws from Madrid were often deferred under the principle “I obey, but I do not carry out”.
lateinamerika#sections.0.paragraphs.1: Brazil was at first granted in hereditary captaincies to private lords; because this model failed, Portugal installed a governor-general in Salvador in 1549. From the 17th century England, France and the Netherlands also set up colonies in the Caribbean whose plantations relied on slave labour. Under Spanish rule Indigenous communities kept their own local leaders, the caciques, who collected tribute and mediated between the village and the colonial state.
lateinamerika#sections.0.paragraphs.2: Independence was carried above all by Creoles, who felt passed over for offices that the Crown preferred to fill with Spaniards. After 1810 republics emerged from long wars, with constitutions modelled on the United States and France; the vote, however, mostly remained limited to men of property. Caudillos, military leaders with a personal following, frequently seized power. The conflict between Conservatives, who supported the Church and tradition, and Liberals, who demanded free trade, secularisation and civil rights, dominated the politics of the 19th century.
lateinamerika#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
lateinamerika#sections.1.paragraphs.0: Colonial society was ordered by origin. At the top stood the Spaniards and Portuguese born in Europe, below them the American-born Creoles, the mestizos with European and Indigenous ancestors, the mulattos, the Indigenous population and the enslaved Africans. In practice this classification was more permeable than on paper: wealth, marriage and parish registers could help decide which group a person belonged to. Nevertheless it determined tax obligations, access to offices and education, and social standing.
lateinamerika#sections.1.paragraphs.1: The Indigenous population collapsed dramatically in the 16th century through epidemics, violence and forced labour; in central Mexico, according to estimates, by far the greater part of the people died within a century. The survivors were gathered into newly laid-out villages and had to pay tribute and perform labour service, but they preserved languages such as Nahuatl, Quechua and Maya as well as many customs. In Brazil and the Caribbean, enslaved Africans and their descendants shaped the population; they worked on sugar plantations, in mines and in households, and created spaces of their own in families, brotherhoods and fugitive communities.
lateinamerika#sections.1.paragraphs.2: In colonial society women had a subordinate legal position, but they could inherit property, run businesses and head households as widows. Convents offered women from wealthy families a place of learning, as the example of the poet Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz shows. Indigenous and African women worked as traders in markets, as domestic servants and in the fields; in the uprising of Túpac Amaru II, Micaela Bastidas took on military and organisational leadership. In the 19th century mass immigration, growing cities and the end of slavery fundamentally changed how people lived together.
lateinamerika#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
lateinamerika#sections.2.paragraphs.0: The spread of Christianity was the declared aim and justification of the conquest. Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Jesuits baptised millions of people and destroyed temples and pictorial manuscripts, but they also learned Indigenous languages, wrote grammars and recorded knowledge about the old cultures, as Bernardino de Sahagún did in his great work on the Aztecs. In popular piety Christian saints merged with older beliefs; devotion to the Virgin of Guadalupe became a symbol of Mexico, and African religions lived on in forms such as Candomblé in Brazil.
lateinamerika#sections.2.paragraphs.1: Members of religious orders argued openly about the legitimacy of the conquest. In 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos denounced the cruelty of the settlers on Hispaniola, and in 1550 Bartolomé de Las Casas defended the human dignity of the Indigenous peoples in the Valladolid debate. These debates contributed to the development of international law as formulated by scholars of the School of Salamanca.
lateinamerika#sections.2.paragraphs.2: In 1551 the first universities on the mainland were founded in Lima and Mexico, and a printing press was already working in Mexico City around 1539. Baroque churches in Mexico, Peru and Brazil combined European forms with Indigenous and African craftsmanship; in Minas Gerais the sculptor Aleijadinho created original masterpieces. In the 19th century writers searched for an identity of their own; in his essay “Our America” of 1891 José Martí called on the peoples of the continent to know themselves and their history instead of imitating Europe and the United States.
lateinamerika#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
lateinamerika#sections.3.paragraphs.0: Silver was the engine of the Spanish colonial economy. Potosí in the Andes and Zacatecas and Guanajuato in Mexico supplied most of the silver mined worldwide between the 16th and 18th centuries. From the 1550s in Mexico and the 1570s at Potosí it was extracted with the amalgamation process, in which mercury drew the silver out of the crushed ore; the poisonous mercury came mainly from Huancavelica in Peru and from Almadén in Spain. Forced labour under the mita system supplied the workers, many of whom died from accidents and poisoning.
